solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Top politician crossing lake with an agricultural worker (9)

indicators.note: PM spans across LOUGH, one on each side of it

annotation.surface: A prime minister strolls by a lake alongside a farmhand, perhaps on a rural photo opportunity.
annotation.walkthrough: The usual lake abbreviation L will not fit; this lake is the Irish spelling of the Scottish loch.
annotation.definitionFit: A ploughman is the farm worker who drives the plough.

clue.text: Fee covering part of play rehearsal (8)

indicators.note: PRICE wraps round ACT like a lid

blocks.note: a play is divided into acts

annotation.surface: A theatre company is charged for an act's rehearsal time.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface runs the three theatre words together, but 'part of play' is its own chunk, ACT, and 'rehearsal' sits apart as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Practice is rehearsal: going over something to get it right.

clue.text: Attack where film stars may be working (5)

definitions.text: where film stars may be working

blocks.note: an old word for an assault or charge

blocks.clueFragment: where film stars may be working
blocks.note: two words: the place where filming happens, with the preposition before it

annotation.surface: An assault breaks out on a location where film stars are shooting.
annotation.walkthrough: The enumeration shows one word, but the second reading needs a space inserted: actors work on the film set. 'Attack' is the older sense, as in the first onset of the enemy.
annotation.definitionFit: Onset once meant an assault, the opening charge against an enemy.

clue.text: Naivete displayed by politician meeting head (9)

indicators.note: GREEN runs straight into NESS, the two joined end to end

blocks.note: a member of the Green Party
a headland, as in Loch Ness's neighbours Dungeness and Sheerness

annotation.surface: A politician's naivety shows when meeting the boss.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Head' is geographic, not the boss: a ness is a headland, familiar from place names such as Dungeness.
annotation.definitionFit: Being green means being inexperienced and naive, so greenness is naivety.

clue.text: Married sailor outside home in charge of hired vehicle (7)

indicators.note: AB stands on the outer end, after the rest

annotation.surface: A married sailor waits outside his house while in charge of a rented car.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Outside' puts AB at the far end rather than wrapping anything; a minicab is a British taxi booked by phone rather than hailed.
annotation.definitionFit: A minicab is a car hired with its driver, like a taxi.

clue.text: Brought up a new perfume in early stages of development (7)

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing up means reading from the bottom, so AN turns to NA

annotation.surface: Someone raised on a new perfume brand in its launch phase.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Brought up' reads like the past of rearing a child; in a down answer it flips the letters beneath it upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Nascent means just coming into being, still in early development.

clue.text: Garden pest a Greek character finally identifies (5)

indicators.note: take only the last letter of identifies

annotation.surface: A Greek man finally names the bug eating his roses.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' is a letter of the alphabet, not a person.
annotation.definitionFit: Aphis is the greenfly or blackfly, an aphid that plagues gardens.

clue.text: Scope of opening move, no good to begin with (5)

indicators.note: remove G (good) from the start

annotation.surface: A chess player judges how far an opening can reach, though it starts badly.
annotation.walkthrough: A gambit is a chess opening that sacrifices a piece; with its opening G gone it leaves AMBIT.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean the range or bounds within which something operates, as in the ambit of a law.

clue.text: Formidable woman’s uncle shakily penning article (9)

indicators.note: something done shakily is unsteady, so the letters of uncle wobble out of their order
the jumbled UNCLE encloses A

annotation.surface: A woman's uncle nervously writes a newspaper piece.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Formidable woman' looks like one phrase for a battleaxe; the definition is just Formidable, and 'woman's' is HER.
annotation.definitionFit: Herculean means requiring great strength, a formidable task like Hercules' labours.

clue.text: Adapted Tamworth accommodation was the tops (6)

blocks.note: the Tamworth is a pig breed, and pigs live in a sty

annotation.surface: Converted housing in the town of Tamworth was top of the range.
annotation.walkthrough: Tamworth is a Staffordshire town, but here it is the ginger pig breed named after it, so its accommodation is a sty.
annotation.definitionFit: Styled means shaped or adapted to a particular design.

clue.text: Passage from a place like Sheppey? (5)

blocks.note: Sheppey is an island in the Thames estuary; the question mark flags it as an example

annotation.surface: A route leading off the Isle of Sheppey in Kent.
annotation.walkthrough: The Isle of Sheppey lies off the north Kent coast; A ISLE runs together into the church passage AISLE.
annotation.definitionFit: An aisle is a passage between rows of seats.

clue.text: Tropical tree sheltering English king twice in battle (9)

indicators.note: NASEBY takes E, R, R under its cover

annotation.surface: A tree in the tropics hid an English king through two battles.
annotation.walkthrough: The battle comes last in the clue but is the outer shell; Naseby was the decisive English Civil War battle of 1645.
annotation.definitionFit: The naseberry is the sapodilla, a tropical evergreen fruit tree.

clue.text: Some thought it a nice vessel once (7)

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the phrase are used

annotation.surface: A few people once admired a ship, a wry nod to how the Titanic was seen before it sank.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is ironic: the Titanic was thought unsinkable, and the answer sits inside the very phrase praising it.
annotation.definitionFit: The Titanic was a liner lost in 1912, a vessel of the past.

clue.text: Wax lyrical in this way visiting east Tyneside region (7)

indicators.note: THUS goes into NE, staying within it

blocks.note: Tyneside is in the North East of England

annotation.surface: Someone raves about a visit to the Newcastle area.
annotation.walkthrough: Tyneside is the area round Newcastle upon Tyne, in the north-east corner of England, so its region is named by a compass abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: To enthuse is to speak with great enthusiasm, to wax lyrical.

clue.text: Financially sound PC spoke resoundingly about that heartlessly (6-8)

indicators.note: about means around, so the loud-speaking word is placed around the letters that follow
without a heart means the middle of the word is cut out, leaving only its two ends

blocks.note: a police constable is a copper
spoke in a loud deep voice

annotation.surface: A police officer declared loudly that a scheme was financially solid.
annotation.walkthrough: PC is not the computer but a police constable; copper is British slang for a police officer.
annotation.definitionFit: Copper-bottomed means thoroughly reliable, especially financially, from ships' copper-sheathed hulls.

clue.text: Outlook for vocal piece that’s turned up on island (9)

indicators.note: in a down clue, SONG reads upwards as GNOS
on means placed upon, and in a down entry what sits on something comes after it, so the island ends the answer

annotation.surface: The prospects for a song that has surfaced on an island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For' is not a link here but PRO, the first chunk.
annotation.definitionFit: A prognosis is a forecast, the outlook for how things will go.

clue.text: Found damaged gate in Rio (9)

indicators.note: the letters are knocked out of order

annotation.surface: A broken gate has been discovered in Rio de Janeiro.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Found' reads as the past of find; the answer needs the verb to found, to establish.
annotation.definitionFit: The verb to found, as in founding a company, means starting something that did not exist before.

clue.text: Chap from Irish county eager at first to tour North Carolina (8)

indicators.note: only the first letter of eager
to tour a place is to go all the way round it, so the county and the letter circle the state

blocks.note: County Clare in the west of Ireland

annotation.surface: An Irishman keen to make a trip round North Carolina.
annotation.walkthrough: The county and the eager letter travel as one unit, and it is that pair, not the E alone, that goes round the state.
annotation.definitionFit: Clarence is a man's name, so any chap might be one.

clue.text: Healthy walk conforming to government policy (14)

blocks.note: a stroll taken for one's health

annotation.surface: A brisk walk that follows the government's line.
annotation.walkthrough: The noun is an old-fashioned name for a daily health walk; the adjective means permitted by the constitution.
annotation.definitionFit: A constitutional is a walk for health; constitutional also means in accordance with a constitution.

clue.text: Vessel Cabot hired regularly when travelling (7)

indicators.note: take every other letter of hired
travelling means moving from place to place, so the letters shift into new positions

annotation.surface: The explorer John Cabot chartered a ship for his regular voyages.
annotation.walkthrough: John Cabot, the Venetian navigator who sailed for England, fits the travelling surface perfectly, but his name is just letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: An iceboat is a vessel, either an icebreaker or a sail craft on runners.

clue.text: Goodness knows how many men put out consuming drug (7)

indicators.note: put out means disturbed or displaced, so these letters are knocked out of their order
the jumble takes E inside

annotation.surface: Countless men were knocked out after taking drugs.
annotation.walkthrough: E is the usual shorthand for the drug ecstasy.
annotation.definitionFit: Umpteen means an indefinitely large number, more than anyone could say.

clue.text: Easy-going police department supporting port authority (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, CID sits beneath PLA

annotation.surface: A relaxed police team backs up the harbour officials.
annotation.walkthrough: The PLA is the Port of London Authority; the CID is the British police's detective branch.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a temperament that is calm and hard to ruffle.

clue.text: Nothing knocked back a lot of keen descendants (7)

indicators.note: something knocked back is pushed backwards, so the word for nothing reads right to left
most but not all of EAGER

annotation.surface: Nothing is drunk, but most of the keen offspring join in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' sounds like drinking; it turns NIL round. 'A lot of' trims only the last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A lineage is a line of descent, the descendants of an ancestor.

clue.text: Doctor abandons hanging fabric — it’s imitation (5)

indicators.note: to abandon is to leave behind, so the doctor walks out of the fabric word and its letters go

annotation.surface: A doctor walks out on curtains that are fake.
annotation.walkthrough: DR is the usual abbreviation for doctor, dropped from the front of DRAPERY.
annotation.definitionFit: The noun comes from to ape, copying someone the way a monkey mimics, so it names the act of imitating.

clue.text: English playwright keeping old dog (7)

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the playwright's name holds the old letter within it

annotation.surface: An English dramatist owns an elderly hound.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old dog' looks like one phrase; 'old' is O inside the playwright, and the definition is just dog.
annotation.definitionFit: A pointer is a gun dog that points at game.

clue.text: Speeds upset US opera, initially proving inappropriate (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, MET is turned over to read TEM
first letters of proving inappropriate

annotation.surface: Tempos upset a New York opera house, first seeming unsuitable.
annotation.walkthrough: The Met is New York's Metropolitan Opera; 'upset' here turns it upside down rather than annoying it.
annotation.definitionFit: Tempi, plural of tempo, are musical speeds.

clue.text: Stew made by idiot in church office (9)

indicators.note: in says the idiot is inside the church, so its letters sit within the church abbreviation

annotation.surface: A fool in the parish office cooks up a stew.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Church office' looks like one place, but 'office' here is a post or function, separate from the church.
annotation.definitionFit: Named after the lidded dish it is cooked in, it is a stew slow-cooked in the oven.

clue.text: A male crew in an Asian capital? (5)

blocks.note: to staff, as in man the boat

annotation.surface: A man joins a team working in one of Asia's capitals.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crew' is a verb, to staff, giving MAN; Amman is the capital of Jordan, in western Asia, hence the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: Amman is the capital of Jordan, which lies in Asia.

clue.text: Attractive second husband involved in home improvements (5)

indicators.note: S and H are put inside DIY

annotation.surface: A good-looking second husband gets stuck into the DIY.
annotation.walkthrough: Dishy is British slang for good-looking, and DIY is do-it-yourself home improvement.
annotation.definitionFit: British informal: someone good-looking is called a dish, and the adjective follows from that.

clue.text: One entering offers third of beef to marinade (9)

indicators.note: entering means going into, so the one goes inside the word for offers
a third of a word here means its third letter, not a third of its length

annotation.surface: A cook adds a third of the beef to a marinade.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Marinade' is used as a verb, to soak meat, and TENDERISE matches it; I enters TENDERS before E completes it.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym by purpose: soaking meat in an acidic liquid softens its fibres, so the one process achieves the other.
